raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils within the myocardium, producing increased ventricular stiffness, atrial dysfunction, conduction disease, microvascular ischemia, and ultimately heart failure [1]. Although many amyloid proteins can involve the heart, contemporary clinical practice is dominated by immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL) and transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), which includes hereditary or variant ATTR (ATTRv) and wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt) [2–4]. This distinction is critical because AL is a hematologic emergency requiring rapid plasma-cell–directed therapy, whereas ATTR-CM is treated by stabilizing transthyretin or reducing hepatic transthyretin production [3,4].

Recognition has increased substantially because ATTR-CM is now understood to be an important cause of “unexplained” heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis, and late-life restrictive cardiomyopathy [5,6]. ATTRwt typically affects older men and is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, atrial fibrillation, and conduction disease; ATTRv may present with cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, or mixed phenotypes depending on the TTR variant [4,7–9]. The Val122Ile/Val142Ile variant is enriched among individuals of African ancestry and is associated with increased heart-failure risk in later life [7]. AL amyloidosis often presents with multiorgan disease—nephrotic proteinuria, autonomic neuropathy, hepatomegaly, macroglossia, purpura—but isolated or predominant cardiac involvement can occur [3].

Clinical suspicion should arise when increased ventricular wall thickness is discordant with electrocardiographic voltage; when heart failure coexists with atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, intolerance of beta-blockers or vasodilators, or persistently elevated troponin; or when echocardiography shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [10]. Cardiac magnetic resonance adds characteristic diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal nulling, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume; transmural enhancement and increasing extracellular volume correlate with amyloid burden and prognosis [14]. Nevertheless, imaging cannot reliably type amyloid, and mistyping can be fatal.

A practical diagnostic algorithm begins with simultaneous evaluation for a monoclonal protein—serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light chains—and bone-avid tracer scintigraphy with technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP [10–13]. In the absence of monoclonal protein, grade 2–3 myocardial uptake on bone scintigraphy can establish ATTR-CM noninvasively; if monoclonal protein is present, biopsy with amyloid typing, preferably by mass spectrometry, is required because AL can occasionally show tracer uptake [11–13]. Once ATTR-CM is diagnosed, TTR sequencing distinguishes ATTRv from ATTRwt and enables family counseling [10]. In AL, cardiac staging with troponin, natriuretic peptides, and involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference stratifies early mortality risk and guides treatment intensity [15,16]. Hematologic and cardiac response criteria based on free light chains and NT-proBNP are essential for monitoring [17].

Management combines heart-failure care, rhythm management, anticoagulation, and disease-modifying therapy. Diuretics remain the cornerstone for congestion, often with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists or sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors when tolerated, but conventional neurohormonal blockade may worsen hypotension or low-output symptoms. Atrial fibrillation is common; because atrial mechanical dysfunction and thrombus can occur even with sinus rhythm, clinicians maintain a low threshold for anticoagulation and transesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion. Pacemakers are frequently needed for conduction disease; defibrillator benefit is less certain because sudden death may reflect electromechanical dissociation rather than shockable arrhythmia.

In AL amyloidosis, urgent clone-directed therapy is the determinant of survival. Daratumumab plus cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone improved hematologic complete response and organ outcomes compared with bortezomib-based therapy alone, establishing a modern first-line standard for eligible patients [18]. Selected low-risk patients may undergo autologous stem-cell transplantation, but advanced cardiac involvement markedly increases treatment-related risk.

For ATTR-CM, tafamidis was the first therapy shown to reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization while slowing functional and quality-of-life decline [19]. Acoramidis, another transthyretin stabilizer, has also shown clinical benefit in ATTR-CM [20]. Gene-silencing therapies are reshaping the field: patisiran improved functional capacity and quality of life in ATTR-CM, and vutrisiran reduced death and recurrent cardiovascular events in a large cardiomyopathy trial [21,22]. Earlier RNA-targeting trials in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy established the biologic feasibility of transthyretin knockdown [23,24]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing has produced deep transthyretin reductions in early studies, but long-term cardiac efficacy and safety remain under investigation [29].

Prognosis depends on amyloid type, disease stage, and timing of therapy. ATTR-CM has a heterogeneous natural history, with staging systems based on NT-proBNP, renal function, and troponin identifying high-risk patients [28,30]. The major contemporary challenge is earlier diagnosis—before advanced restrictive physiology, frailty, renal dysfunction, and irreversible organ damage—so that disease-modifying therapies can be deployed when benefit is greatest [25–27].
